extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science; readers interested in party machines and urban politics
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length analytical description of how party machines, rings, and bosses operate in urban and state politics, including their causes, organization, methods, and sources of revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan chairman's decisive role in credentials disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: In doubtful cases a partisan chairman is valuable, for, as it is expressed, 'he is a solid 8 to 7 man all the time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that when credential fights arise at primaries or conventions the chairman's partisanship can determine exclusion/admission of delegates; chairman can influence outcomes via disorder or procedural manoeuvres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prearranged nominations and packed conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the convention has been properly packed, he is nominated by acclamation... Everything had evidently been prearranged; and the discontented, if any there were, had been talked over during the swarming hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how party managers predetermine candidates by controlling primaries/delegates and arranging backstage agreements so public proceedings merely ratify choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification meetings are symbolic not practical
rubrics_metrics.description: A gathering, called a 'ratification' meeting, has no practical importance, being attended only by those prepared to support the nominations made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that post-convention public meetings serve to publicly adopt decisions already made by managers; they do not affect nomination outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural causes enabling the Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The elective offices are so numerous that ordinary citizens cannot watch them... conventions come so often that busy men cannot serve in them... the primary lists are so contrived that only a fraction of the party get on them... the mass of the voters are ignorant; knowing nothing about the personal merits of the candidates, they are ready to follow their leaders like sheep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies concrete institutional and social conditions (many offices, frequent conventions, unattractive minor posts, contrived primaries, voter ignorance and party loyalty) that make machine control feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career path of the worker ('the Boys') into machine service
rubrics_metrics.description: He becomes a member of his primary, attends regularly, attaches himself to some leader... renders service by voting as his leader wishes, and by doing duty at elections... he is chosen delegate to a convention... appointed to some petty office... rises to sit on the central committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps how local influence, loyal service, and small rewards (jobs/places) create a class of dependable workers who supply the machine's manpower and can be promoted into party structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of a Ring
rubrics_metrics.description: They cement their dominion by combination... Such a combination is called a Ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that a Ring is a coalition of leaders who coordinate to control primaries, select candidates, run conventions, organize elections, and secure statutes that protect their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of the Boss
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the Ring... dispenses places, rewards the loyal, punishes the mutinous, concocts schemes, negotiates treaties. He generally avoids publicity, preferring the substance to the pomp of power, and is all the more dangerous because he sits, like a spider, hidden in the midst of his web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the Boss as the dominant individual who centralizes control, exercises patronage, and operates largely behind the scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between city Boss and State Boss
rubrics_metrics.description: A great city is the best soil for the growth of a Boss... a State Boss... dictates State nominations, and through his lieutenants controls State and sometimes Congressional conventions... The State Boss is usually, almost necessarily, a member of Congress, probably a senator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains differences in scope, required abilities, and leverage (e.g., Congressional influence) between city-level and state-level bosses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boss' required arts and social disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: What he needs are the arts of intrigue and that knowledge of men which teaches him when to bully, when to cajole... A Boss ought therefore to be hail fellow well met, those who frequent these places, not fastidious in his tastes, fond of a drink and willing to stand one, jovial in manners, and ready to oblige even a humble friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies interpersonal skills, rough social ease, and familiarity with committee-rooms and saloons as practical assets for a Boss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social venues (saloons) for political organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower sort of city politicians congregate in clubs and bar-rooms... Of the 1007 primaries and conventions... held in New York City preparatory to the elections of 1884, 633 took place in liquor saloons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how social gathering places serve as meeting sites and recruitment grounds for workers and how venue choice reinforces cohesion and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slate creation, dickering, and the Deal
rubrics_metrics.description: Some leading man... sketches out an allotment of places... results in a Slate... By a process of 'dickering' (i.e. bargaining by way of barter), various offers and suggestions being made all round, a list is settled on which the high contracting parties agree. This is a Deal, or Trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the backstage bargaining among leaders to allocate offices and produce a slate presented to the convention; 'breaking the slate' and schism are risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing primaries and running the ticket through conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The accepted slate is now ready to be turned by the Machine into a Ticket... the comparatively easy process of getting the proper delegates chosen by packed primaries, and running the various parts of the ticket through the conventions...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the tactical process of securing compliant delegate majorities (packing) to ensure slate nomination across multiple stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict party discipline and internal moral code
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline is very strict in this army... It does not forbid falsehood, or malversation, or ballot stuffing... But it denounces apathy or cowardice, disobedience, and above all, treason to the party. Its typical virtue is 'solidity,' unity of heart, mind, and effort among the workers, unquestioning loyalty to the party leaders, and devotion to the party ticket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that the party's internal ethic prizes unity and obedience over legal or civic virtues; dissenters are labeled 'Kicker or Bolter' and punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishments and reprisals against dissenters
rubrics_metrics.description: He who takes his own course is a Kicker or Bolter; and is punished not only sternly but vindictively. The path of promotion is closed to him; he is turned out of the primary, and forbidden to hope for a delegacy to a convention; he is dismissed from any office he holds which the Ring can command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the concrete sanctions (exclusion, dismissal, loss of promotion) imposed to enforce conformity; mentions dark tales of secret police and disappearances as alleged extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public employees as a mobilized party force
rubrics_metrics.description: There are more than forty thousand persons employed by the city authorities... the large majority dismissible by their superiors at short notice... If the same party happens to be supreme in city politics, in the Federal government, and in the State government, all this army of employees is expected to work for the party leaders of the city, in city primaries, conventions, and elections, and is virtually amenable to the orders of these leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how patronage employment creates a large, disciplinable labour force available for party mobilization and electoral tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service rules exist but are limited in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Statutes and Civil Service rules made under them now provide that no person in the public service shall be compelled to contribute service or money for political purposes... These rules, however, do not cover the whole field, and it is believed that they are not always observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the presence of legal/regulatory constraints on using public servants politically, but emphasizes gaps in coverage and imperfect compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of Ring revenue — public subscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: I. The first is public subscriptions. For important elections such as the biennial elections of State officers... a 'campaign fund' is raised by an appeal to wealthy members of the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains regular fundraising appeals to party-aligned wealthy individuals to build a campaign fund; reflects strong party feeling that motivates contributions even from critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of Ring revenue — private contributions from rich men and corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: II. Contributions are sometimes privately obtained from rich men and especially from corporations (though statutes are now attempting to prevent this) who... may expect something from its action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights corporate and wealthy patronage as a significant but legally contested funding source tied to anticipated favors (contracts, legislation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of Ring revenue — surreptitious appropriation from public treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: III. An exceptionally audacious Ring has been known to make a surreptitious appropriation from the city or (more rarely) from the State treasury for the purposes... of its own election funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes illicit embezzlement/manipulation of public accounts to hide election-related expenditures; only possible where Ring controls public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of Ring revenue — tax on office-holders' salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: IV. A tax used to be levied upon the office-holders of the party, varying from one to four or even five per cent upon the amount of their annual salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains systemic assessments of officials' salaries as a steady revenue stream for election expenses; provides numerical examples and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-party trading and pragmatic co-operation between bosses
rubrics_metrics.description: Accordingly it sometimes happens that there is a good understanding between the chiefs of opposite parties in cities; they will even go the length of making a joint 'deal,' i.e. of arranging for a distribution of offices whereby some of the friends of one shall get places, the residue being left for the friends of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that bosses may forge cross-party bargains to allocate spoils pragmatically; such arrangements are usually private and hard to prove.
